Current synthesis: A is unassailable compliant. B is non-compliant on majority Canadian-bank reading, compliant on Colleague 6’s straight issuer-based bank-debt reading. D is non-compliant on majority debt-only reading, potentially compliant on Colleague 4’s issuer-based securities-wide reading. C is treated by majority as compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with financials as distractor, subject to private-issuer predicate establishment. E is compliant under the cooperative member exemption on conventional membership assumption, less secure if membership is not expressly made out. Unresolved: precise wording/scope of s.2.35/2.36 re foreign banks and debt-only vs equity; factual sufficiency of private-issuer predicates for C; and factual sufficiency of membership for E.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Thanks everyone, this is a very helpful close read and the issuer-based / retail-permissive framing you’re all laying out for the financial institution exemptions is the thing I’m hanging on to.

I agree with Colleagues 1,2,3 and 5 that NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.36 and the OSA s.73 financial institution carve-out is issuer based and is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor status, purchaser net worth, income or the size of the distribution. That is why the large retail pool and the zero net assets / unemployed purchaser facts are being treated as immaterial for the bank bond examples.

That issuer-based rationale is what makes me pause on the debt-only gloss that is being used to knock out D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I Bank Act bank. If the policy that drives s.2.35/2.36 is really “the exemption attaches to the regulated financial institution status of the issuer and is not conditioned on the purchaser’s wealth”, then the purchaser’s $0 net assets and unemployment status is irrelevant for Fairstone on exactly the same logic that makes the retail bond distribution for Bank of China Canada look clean.

Can we confirm the exact statutory wording we’re applying for s.2.35/2.36? The teaching version is “non-convertible debt securities of a bank / loan corporation / trust company / insurance company”. If the text is expressly limited to debt securities, D is out as equity. If the operative framing in the Ontario rule is “securities of a bank”, the equity vs debt distinction starts to look like a policy gloss imported from the commercial paper context rather than a condition written into the exemption, and Fairstone’s share distribution would be on the same issuer-based footing as A.

That also helps sort the other options. E is the classic co-operative credit association / caisse populaire member share exemption under NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 and purchaser wealth is indeed irrelevant there, but the facts as stated say “a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed” and do not state a membership relationship to Caisse populaire acadienne ltée. Without the members-only condition made out on the facts, E is less secure than the issuer-based bank analysis.

C is a good illustration of the private issuer s.2.4 distractor at work – the $35k salary / $10k net assets are clearly there to defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM eligible investor analysis – but the facts do not establish the NI 45-106 private issuer predicates, e.g. non-reporting issuer and <50 holders worldwide, no advertising, ≤50 purchasers in 12 months. The financials are a distractor, but they are not proof the s.2.4 conditions are met.

B remains the cleanest difficulty on the Canadian Bank Act issuer point, which is why I think the real tension in the set is between A and D under the same issuer-based bank reading, and whether we are reading a debt-only carve-out into s.2.35/2.36 or sticking with the issuer-based text. I’d like us to lock down the precise wording of s.2.35(1)/s.2.36(1) on debt securities vs securities of a bank before we treat the debt-only reading as decisive for D.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the core framing that has emerged in rounds 1-2: NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer based, retail permissive and contains no accredited/eligible investor or purchaser financial test for non-convertible debt of a financial institution. Purchaser net worth, employment status and the number of purchasers are immaterial under that exemption, which is why the zero-net-asset/unemployed fact patterns are distractors for the bank-debt analysis.

On that basis A is the textbook illustration: Bank of China [Canada] is a Schedule II Bank Act bank and a non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors in Ontario is comfortably within s.2.35/2.36.

My lingering uncertainty is the Canadian-bank filter that is being imported into the application of s.2.35/2.36 to B. The issuer-based, purchaser-condition-free logic we are all using for A is doing a lot of work, and s.2.35/2.36 on its face speaks to “debt securities of a bank”. JPMorgan Chase is a bank and the securities at issue are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt securities. The fact pattern is a non-prospectus distribution of those bonds aimed at a large number of Canadian investors, i.e. the classic retail debt fact pattern the exemption is written for.

The “Bank Act bank / Schedule I/II/III / authorised foreign bank Canadian presence” limitation is how the exemption is usually taught, but it is a policy gloss read into the definition of bank in NI 45-106. On a straight issuer-based reading s.2.35/2.36 does not expressly require Schedule I/II/III listing and does not on its face condition the exemption on where the issuer is incorporated, only that the issuer is a bank issuing debt. If we accept the issuer-based, retail-permissive rationale for A, the textual distinction between Bank of China Canada and JPMorgan Chase is incorporation rather than the statutory elements of debt of a bank issued without a prospectus to retail.

That statutory ambiguity matters because the room is already crowded with more than one apparently viable exemption. Colleagues 1,2,3,5 now treat C as capable under NI 45-106 s.2.4 private issuer, with the $35k salary/$10k net assets being the s.2.3 / s.2.9 distractor, and E as viable under NI 45-106 s.2.34 member share exemption. E is in fact less secure on the facts as written: the fact pattern states “a large number of retail investors” not “members” of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée, and the credit-union/caisse populaire exemption is member based. Without an express members-only condition made out E is a residual rather than a solid exemplar.

With C viable on a private-issuer reading, E weakened by the missing membership predicate, and a plausible textual argument that the bank-debt exemption is issuer based and not expressly Canada-only, B looks textually as clean an illustration of the retail-permissive debt exemption as A, and the question is not pointing to a single unambiguously unique compliant distribution. That is why I am uncomfortable treating A as the sole exemplar and the Canadian-bank incorporation point as dispositive for B.

5.text:
Ontario s.53 OSA is displaced in January 2020 by NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501 and Ont.Reg.1015.

Bank non-convertible debt
NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is an issuer based, retail permissive exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company and insurance company. “Bank” in NI 45-106 is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada. The exemption is not conditioned on accredited/eligible status, purchaser net worth or the number of purchasers.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors is the textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank debt exemption. Retail solicitation and a large number of purchasers are immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant.
* B. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent holding company. On the facts stated there is no Bank Act issuer and no Canadian branch issuer made out, and no other exemption is made out. The bank debt exemption is limited to debt of a Bank Act bank. B is a prospectus distribution in Ontario.

Private issuer
NI 45-106 s.2.4 is an issuer based private issuer exemption. It requires a private issuer i.e. non-reporting <50 holders worldwide, ≤50 purchasers in 12 months and no advertising. It does not impose an accredited/eligible investor or minimum amount financial test.

* C. The facts state the distribution is by a private issuer to a non-connected individual purchaser. Salary $35k / net assets $10k defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM eligible investor and are therefore the intended distractor for s.2.4. On the stated private-issuer predicate the trade is capable of / is made under s.2.4. It would not be exempt under s.2.3/s.2.9, which is why the financials are present.

Bank equity v bank debt
The financial institution exemption is debt only. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not caught by s.2.35/2.36.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I Bank Act bank. Its non-convertible debt would be exempt, its equity is not. A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family/friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is non-exempt. The issuer-based rationale does not convert s.2.35/2.36 into an equity exemption.

Co-operative credit association / caisse populaire
NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based issuer exemption for distributions of securities by a Canadian cooperative credit association/caisse populaire to its members. It is not subject to accredited/eligible financial tests.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. On the classic teaching the member share offering is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ net worth/employment, so the $0 net assets/unemployed fact is irrelevant. The exemption is made out on the standard membership assumption; the residual factual caveat rightly flagged by Colleague 4 is that the facts are worded as “retail investors” and do not expressly state a membership relationship.

On the statutory text as applied in January 2020 the unassailable archetypal compliant transaction in the set is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. On a straight NI 45-106 reading C is compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with the financials as a distractor, and E is compliant under the s.2.34 member exemption subject to the membership condition. B and D are non-compliant on the conventional Bank Act bank and debt-only readings.

2.text:
Ontario s.53 OSA prospectus obligation is displaced in Jan 2020 by NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501 and Ont Reg 1015.

Bank non-convertible debt

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is an issuer based, retail permissive, non-convertible debt security exemption. “Bank” in NI 45-106 s.1.1 is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada. The exemption is not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor status or on purchaser net worth.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors in Ontario is the textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank debt exemption. The large retail pool and the retail nature of the offering are immaterial. A is unassailable.

* B. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent. On the facts as stated there is no Bank Act issuer, no Canadian branch issuer and no guarantee by a Canadian bank made out and no other exemption is made out. The bank debt exemption is limited to debt of a bank to which the Bank Act applies. B is a prospectus distribution in Ontario.

Private issuer

NI 45-106 s.2.4 is an issuer based private issuer exemption. The exemption does not impose an accredited investor, eligible investor or minimum amount financial test on the purchaser. The salary $35k / net assets $10k figures defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM/eligible investor analyses and are properly a distractor for s.2.4.

* C. The fact pattern states the distribution is by a private issuer to a single non-connected purchaser. On a straight statutory reading s.2.4 is capable of being available and the $35k/$10k financials are irrelevant to s.2.4. It would not be exempt under s.2.3 or s.2.9 and s.2.5 family/friends is not available, which is why the financials are present. C is capable/compliant under s.2.4 subject to the usual private issuer predicates being met – non-reporting, <50 holders worldwide, no advertising and ≤50 purchasers in 12 months – which are not negatived on the facts.

Bank equity v bank debt

The financial institution exemption in s.2.35/2.36 is debt only.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Bank Act bank; its non-convertible debt would be within s.2.35/2.36, its equity is not. A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is a prospectus distribution.

Co-operative credit association

NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based, issuer based exemption for distributions of securities by a co-operative credit association/caisse populaire to its members. It is not subject to accredited/eligible financial tests.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. The exemption is real and purchaser wealth is irrelevant, but it is membership based. The facts as worded say “a large number of retail investors” and do not expressly state a members-only distribution to members of the association. Without the membership condition being made out on the facts as stated the s.2.34 exemption is not made out. On the conventional teaching assumption that a caisse populaire offering is to members, E would be compliant, the $0 net assets/unemployed fact being irrelevant.

On that statutory reading the only uncontroversially compliant example in the list is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. B and D are non-exempt on the majority reading, C is exempt under s.2.4 with the financials as a distractor and E is compliant under the co-operative member exemption subject to the express membership condition noted above.

Ontario prospectus is s.53 OSA as displaced in Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015.

* Bank non-convertible debt
NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is an issuer based, retail permissive, debt only exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank / loan corporation / trust company / insurance company to which the Bank Act, Canada applies. B. The s.2.35/2.36 bank is defined in NI 45-106 as a bank listed in Schedule I/II/III of the Bank Act, Canada. On the facts as stated the issuer is JPMorgan Chase the U.S. parent, with a general Canadian retail bond offering and no Bank Act issuer or Canadian authorized foreign bank Canadian presence made out. No other exemption is made out on the facts. On the statutory Canadian-bank reading B is a prospectus distribution in Ontario. The “any bank” reading advanced by Colleague 6 is the outlier.

* Private issuer
NI 45-106 s.2.4 is an issuer based private issuer exemption. The issuer must be a private issuer, non reporting and <50 holders worldwide, the distribution must be to ≤50 purchasers in 12 months and not by advertising. There is no accredited/ eligible investor financial test in s.2.4.

C. The facts state the distribution is by a private issuer to a single non connected purchaser. Salary $35k and net assets $10k defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 Ontario offering memorandum / eligible investor and they are properly a distractor for s.2.4. On the stated private issuer predicate the trade is capable of / is made under s.2.4, subject to the usual private issuer / no advertising / purchaser count conditions which are not negatived on the facts. C is therefore compliant under s.2.4, the financials being irrelevant to s.2.4.

* Bank equity v bank debt
The financial institution exemption is debt only. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not caught by s.2.35/2.36.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I bank. Its non-convertible debt would be within s.2.35/2.36; its equity is not. A non prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/ eligible/ OM/ minimum amount/ family friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is a prospectus distribution. The “securities of a bank” reading advanced by Colleague 4 would convert a debt exemption into an equity exemption and is not supported by s.2.35/2.36.

* Cooperative credit association / caisse populaire
NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based, issuer based exemption for distributions of securities by a cooperative credit association / caisse populaire to its members. Purchaser wealth is irrelevant.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. On the usual teaching a member share offering is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ net worth/employment and the $0 net assets/unemployed fact is therefore irrelevant. The exemption is made out on the conventional member based reading. The residual factual point rightly flagged by Colleague 4 is the express membership condition: the fact pattern states “a large number of retail investors” rather than members. On a strict reading of the facts as given the membership condition is not proved, whereas on the conventional caisse populaire fact pattern the exemption is made out.

On that basis the unassailable, archetypal compliant transaction in the set is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. B and D are non-exempt on the majority statutory reading. C is compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with the financial details as distractors, and E is compliant under the cooperative member share exemption on the standard membership assumption. If an unambiguous answer on the facts as stated is required, A is the only option that is made out without factual assumptions.

Without an express members-only condition made out E is a residual rather than a solid exemplar.

With C viable on a private-issuer reading, E weakened by the missing membership predicate, and a plausible textual argument that the bank-debt exemption is issuer based and not expressly Canada-only, B looks textually as clean an illustration of the retail-permissive debt exemption as A, and the question is not pointing to a single unambiguously unique compliant distribution. That is why I am uncomfortable treating A as the sole exemplar and the Canadian-bank incorporation point as dispositive for B.

Ontario s.53 OSA is displaced in January 2020 by NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501 and Ont.Reg.1015.

Bank non-convertible debt
NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is an issuer based, retail permissive exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company and insurance company. “Bank” in NI 45-106 is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada. The exemption is not conditioned on accredited/eligible status, purchaser net worth or the number of purchasers.

* A. Bank of China Canada is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors is the textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank debt exemption. Retail solicitation and a large number of purchasers are immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant.
* B. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent holding company. On the facts stated there is no Bank Act issuer and no Canadian branch issuer made out, and no other exemption is made out. The bank debt exemption is limited to debt of a Bank Act bank. B is a prospectus distribution in Ontario.

Private issuer
NI 45-106 s.2.4 is an issuer based private issuer exemption. It requires a private issuer i.e. non-reporting <50 holders worldwide, ≤50 purchasers in 12 months and no advertising. It does not impose an accredited/eligible investor or minimum amount financial test.

* C. The facts state the distribution is by a private issuer to a non-connected individual purchaser. Salary $35k / net assets $10k defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM eligible investor and are therefore the intended distractor for s.2.4. On the stated private-issuer predicate the trade is capable of / is made under s.2.4. It would not be exempt under s.2.3/s.2.9, which is why the financials are present.

Bank equity v bank debt
The financial institution exemption is debt only. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not caught by s.2.35/2.36.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I Bank Act bank. Its non-convertible debt would be exempt, its equity is not. A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net asset unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family/friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is non-exempt. The issuer-based rationale does not convert s.2.35/2.36 into an equity exemption.

Co-operative credit association / caisse populaire
NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based issuer exemption for distributions of securities by a Canadian cooperative credit association/caisse populaire to its members. It is not subject to accredited/eligible financial tests.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. On the classic teaching the member share offering is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ net worth/employment, so the $0 net assets/unemployed fact is irrelevant. The exemption is made out on the standard membership assumption; the residual factual caveat rightly flagged by Colleague 4 is that the facts are worded as “retail investors” and do not expressly state a membership relationship.

On the statutory text as applied in January 2020 the unassailable archetypal compliant transaction in the set is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. On a straight NI 45-106 reading C is compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with the financials as a distractor, and E is compliant under the s.2.34 member exemption subject to the membership condition. B and D are non-compliant on the conventional Bank Act bank and debt-only readings.

A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is a prospectus distribution.

Co-operative credit association

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Ontario prospectus s.53 OSA displaced Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015.

Bank non-convertible debt exemption NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer-based, retail-permissive, purchaser-condition-free for non-convertible debt of a bank/loan/trust/insurance. NI 45-106 definition of “bank” = Schedule I/II/III Bank Act, Canada. Exemption is debt only.

A. Bank of China (Canada) Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds to retail. Unanimous majority: textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank-debt exemption, unambiguously compliant. No serious dispute.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to large Canadian retail pool.
Majority 1,2,3,5: exemption requires Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank Canadian presence; U.S. parent on facts as stated is outside s.2.35/2.36 and no other exemption made out → prospectus required, non-compliant.
Minority Colleague 6: reads s.2.35/2.36 as issuer-based “debt securities of a bank” with no Canada-only incorporation condition; JPMorgan Chase is a bank and bonds are debt → would be exempt. Disagreement persists on foreign bank scope / Canadian nexus. Colleague 6 argues Schedule I/II/III limitation is policy gloss, not statutory text.

C. Private issuer shares to non-connected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k CAD.
Accredited investor NI 31-103 not met; eligible investor NI 45-106 s.2.9 not met; family/friends s.2.5 not available.
Majority 1,2,3,5 in current round: NI 45-106 s.2.4 private issuer exemption is issuer-based, no accredited/eligible financial test, ≤50 purchasers / no advertising conditions. Facts state “private issuer” and one purchaser; salary/net assets are distractors for accredited/OM analysis. Hence capable/compliant under s.2.4.
Remaining concern raised by Colleague 4: private issuer predicates – non-reporting, <50 holders worldwide, no advertising, ≤50 purchasers – not expressly proven on facts; financials are distractor but not proof conditions met.

D. Shares without prospectus by Fairstone Bank of Canada to large retail pool including purchaser $0 net assets unemployed.
Majority 1,2,3,5: s.2.35/2.36 is debt only. Equity not covered. No accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption made out → prospectus required, non-compliant.
Colleague 4 dissent: issuer-based rationale for bank exemption should attach to Fairstone as a Schedule I bank irrespective of debt vs equity; purchaser wealth irrelevant. Core disagreement is debt-only vs “securities of a bank” reading of s.2.35/2.36. Colleague 4 asks for exact wording of s.2.35(1)/s.2.36(1) to confirm debt limitation.

E. Shares without prospectus by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée to large retail pool including purchaser $0 net assets unemployed.
Majority 1,2,3,5: cooperative credit association / caisse populaire member-share exemption NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34, OSA s.73, issuer and member based, no accredited/eligible test; purchaser wealth irrelevant.
Colleague 4 notes membership requirement not stated; facts say “large number of retail investors” not “members”. Without express members-only condition made out on facts as stated, s.2.34 not proved; on conventional membership assumption E would be compliant.

Unresolved / tracking:
- Foreign bank scope for bank-debt exemption: Canadian Bank Act bank required or any bank sufficient? Majority = Canadian nexus; minority Colleague 6 = any bank.
- Bank exemption covers equity? Majority = debt only; minority Colleague 4 = securities of bank, issuer-based.
- Membership condition for E: is it satisfied on facts? Majority assumes yes; Colleague 4 flags missing.
- Private issuer exemption for C: are issuer status/conditions established, or are financials merely distractors vs evidence issuer is not private? Current majority treats as compliant under s.2.4.

Current best synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. B is majority non-compliant, minority compliant. D is majority non-compliant, minority compliant. E is majority compliant under cooperative member exemption subject to membership assumption. C is majority now viewed as compliant under s.2.4 private issuer, financial details distractors. Archetypal compliant example remains A.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Shared baseline unchanged: Ontario prospectus s.53 OSA displaced Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015. Financial institution exemptions are issuer based, retail permissive, no purchaser wealth test.

Bank debt
* A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail without prospectus. Uncontested compliant. Bank of China Canada is Schedule II Bank Act bank; NI 45-106 s.2.35 and Rule 45-501 s.2.36 non-convertible debt of a Bank Act bank is issuer based, retail permitted, no accredited/eligible test. Large retail pool immaterial.
* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to large Canadian investors without prospectus. Majority 1,2,3,5: exemption limited to debt securities of a bank to which the Bank Act applies, i.e. Schedule I/II/III Canadian bank or authorised foreign bank acting through Canadian presence. JPMorgan Chase is U.S. parent, no Canadian Bank Act issuer or branch issuance made out, no other exemption stated → non-exempt. Minority Colleague 6 persists: s.2.35/2.36 is textually “debt securities of a bank”, issuer based and purchaser-condition free, does not on its face require Canadian incorporation; on straight reading B is as compliant as A. Disagreement remains on foreign-bank scope.

Private issuer / accredited / OM
* C – shares by private issuer to non-connected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Majority 1,2,3,5 in current round now treat financials as distractor and rely on NI 45-106 s.2.4 private issuer exemption: issuer based, no accredited/eligible financial test, 50 purchaser/no-advertising conditions not negatived. On that reading C is capable of being exempt; would not be exempt under s.2.3 accredited investor or s.2.9 eligible investor/OM. Colleague 4 continues factual predicate challenge: facts do not establish private issuer status in NI 45-106 sense <50 holders non-reporting nor advertising limits, so exemption not made out on facts. Change from round 0 accredited-only view now largely abandoned by majority.

Bank equity
* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares without prospectus to broad retail including $0 net assets unemployed purchaser. Majority 1,2,3,5: financial institution exemption is debt only; equity not caught by s.2.35/2.36; no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount exemption made out → non-exempt. Colleague 4 dissent persists: issuer-based rationale of bank exemption suggests securities of a bank not debt-limited; purchaser wealth irrelevant; on that reading D would be compliant irrespective of equity status. Outlier issuer-based securities view remains.

Credit union / co-operative
* E – shares by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée to large retail pool including $0 net assets unemployed purchaser. Majority 1,2,3,5: prospectus exemption NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 for distributions by Canadian co-operative credit association/caisse populaire to members, issuer and member based, no accredited/eligible test, purchaser wealth irrelevant. Residual caveat: exemption is member based. Fact pattern states “retail investors” not expressly members. Colleague 4 and 5 flag membership condition; if membership not established exemption may fail. On conventional teaching membership assumed.

Unresolved / to track
* Scope of bank debt exemption for authorized foreign banks vs U.S. parent issuer for B, and whether statutory text requires Canadian Bank Act bank.
* Whether private issuer exemption s.2.4 can be relied on for C given lack of explicit facts on <50 holders, reporting status, no-advertising/50 purchaser limits.
* Whether credit union exemption for E requires membership and whether fact pattern satisfies it; factual wording “retail investors” vs “members”.
* Debt vs equity scope of bank exemption driving D disagreement, and Colleague 4’s issuer-based securities reading.

Current working synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. E is widely treated as compliant under co-operative member exemption subject to membership condition. C is majority-leaning compliant under private issuer exemption with financials as distractor, though factual predicates contested. B and D are majority non-compliant; B has persistent minority compliant view on foreign bank scope, D has minority issuer-based securities compliant view.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Ontario prospectus obligation s.53 OSA is displaced in Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015. The financial institution debt exemption NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer based, retail permissive, non-convertible debt only, and not conditioned on accredited/eligible investor status or purchaser net worth.

A. Bank of China [Canada] bonds without prospectus to retail investors. Bank of China Canada is Schedule II Bank Act bank. Non-convertible debt of a Bank Act bank is textbook exempt. Unanimous compliant. Colleagues 1,2,3,5,6 agree A is unassailable archetypal compliant.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds without prospectus to large Canadian investor pool. Majority 1,2,3,5: s.2.35/2.36 “bank” is a bank to which the Bank Act applies, i.e., Schedule I/II/III Canadian bank or authorised foreign bank acting through Canadian presence. JPMorgan Chase is US parent issuer on facts; no Canadian Bank Act issuer/branch/guarantee made out and no other exemption stated → prospectus required. Colleague 6 dissents: s.2.35/2.36 is phrased as debt securities of a bank, issuer based, purchaser-condition free, does not on its face say “Canadian bank”. On straight textual issuer-based debt reading JPMorgan Chase is a bank and bonds are debt, so B would be as compliant as A. Foreign-bank/Canadian-incorporation scope remains open; this is the main textual ambiguity.

C. Private issuer shares to non-connected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Accredited investor NI 31-103 and Ontario eligible investor NI 45-106 s.2.9 thresholds not met: $35k < $200k/$75k, $10k < $1M/$400k. Family/friends s.2.5 not available. NI 45-106 s.2.4 private issuer exemption is issuer based: issuer must be private, non-reporting, <50 holders worldwide, ≤50 purchasers/12m, no advertising, no purchaser financial test. Fact pattern states “by a private issuer”. Majority 1,2,3,5 now treat s.2.4 as available and salary/net asset figures as distractors for accredited/eligible analysis. Colleague 4 notes facts do not establish private-issuer predicates <50 holders/no advertising/50 purchaser limit. Whether Ontario Jan 2020 practice treats s.2.4 as unconditional for a truly unconnected purchaser remains an open gloss point; current majority treats C as capable/compliant under s.2.4, subject to predicate establishment.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada shares without prospectus to broad retail including $0 net assets unemployed purchaser. Majority 1,2,3,5: financial institution exemption is debt only. Fairstone Bank is Bank Act bank; its debt would be exempt under s.2.35/2.36, its equity is not. No accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption made out → prospectus required. Colleague 4 dissents: issuer-based rationale that purchaser wealth is irrelevant under bank exemption suggests a securities-wide bank exemption; on that reading D would be defensible on same rationale as A. Debt-only vs securities-wide reading of s.2.35/2.36 and OSA s.73 unresolved, with majority reading debt-only. Colleague 4 also asks to confirm exact statutory wording debt securities vs securities of a bank.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée shares without prospectus to large retail pool including $0 net assets unemployed purchaser. NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is cooperative credit association/caisse populaire member-share exemption, issuer based and member based, no accredited/eligible test. Majority assumes membership is implicit for a caisse populaire offering and treats E as compliant irrespective of purchaser wealth. Colleague 4 and Colleague 6 flag factual gap: facts state “retail investors” not expressly “members”; without a members-only distribution exemption is not made out on facts as stated. Membership condition is residual caveat for E.

Current synthesis: A is unassailable compliant. B is non-compliant on majority Canadian-bank reading, compliant on Colleague 6’s straight issuer-based bank-debt reading. C is treated by majority as compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with financials as distractor, subject to private-issuer predicate establishment noted by Colleague 4 / Colleague 2. D is non-compliant on majority debt-only reading, potentially compliant on Colleague 4’s issuer-based securities-wide reading. E is compliant under cooperative member exemption on conventional membership assumption, less secure if membership not expressly made out. Unresolved: precise wording/scope of s.2.35/2.36 re foreign banks and debt-only vs equity; factual sufficiency of private-issuer predicates for C; and factual sufficiency of membership for E.

reflection_text.1:
Ontario prospectus s.53 OSA displaced Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015.

reflection_text.3:

Bank debt

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Thanks for the detailed close reads – the issuer-based, retail-permissive, no purchaser wealth test framing for the financial institution carve-out is now the shared anchor in the room and that’s the right anchor.

I agree with Colleagues 1,2,3 and 5 that NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer based and not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor status or on net worth. That is why the large retail pool and the zero net assets / unemployed purchaser facts are properly treated as distractors for a bank debt analysis.

That shared framing is what makes me uneasy with treating the Canadian Bank Act limitation as dispositive for B. s.2.35/2.36 on its face speaks to non-convertible debt securities of a bank. JPMorgan Chase is a bank and the securities at issue are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt securities, distributed without a prospectus to a large number of Canadian investors. The elements of the exemption — bank issuer, debt security, non-prospectus retail distribution — are all made out on the facts.

The Schedule I/II/III gloss is the usual teaching shorthand for the definition of “bank” in NI 45-106 s.1.1, but the exemption text itself does not on its face condition the exemption on Canadian incorporation or on a Canadian authorized branch issuance. In an issuer-based, purchaser-condition-free regime, the textual distinction between Bank of China Canada and JPMorgan Chase is incorporation, not the statutory elements of debt of a bank issued without a prospectus to retail. On a straight statutory reading B is textually as clean an illustration of the retail-permissive bank debt exemption as A, and it tests the foreign bank extension of the same issuer-based logic we are all using for A.

That matters because the other alternatives you have all helpfully surfaced are not unambiguously made out on the facts as stated.

E is the classic co-operative credit association / caisse populaire member share exemption under NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 and purchaser wealth is irrelevant there, but the exemption is member based. The fact pattern states “a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed” and does not state a members-only distribution to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée. Without the express membership condition made out on the facts as written, E is weakened relative to a straightforward bank debt analysis.

C is a good private issuer s.2.4 distractor — the $35k salary / $10k net assets clearly defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM eligible investor — but the facts do not establish the NI 45-106 private issuer predicates: non-reporting, <50 holders worldwide, no advertising and ≤50 purchasers in 12 months. The financials are a distractor, but they are not proof the s.2.4 conditions are met.

D remains equity, not debt, and the majority position that s.2.35/2.36 is debt only is well supported; Fairstone Bank common shares to retail including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no other exemption is made out.

Given that, with E weakened by the missing membership predicate and C lacking stated private issuer predicates, the real tension in the set is between the two bank debt examples. If we take the issuer-based, retail-permissive rationale seriously, B is not an outlier; it is a plausible, textually faithful application of the same exemption we are invoking for A. That is why I am leaning toward B as the intended illustration of the bank debt carve-out under the issuer-based reading the room has converged on.

5.text:
Ontario prospectus liability is s.53 OSA as displaced in Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015.

* Bank non-convertible debt
NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer based and retail permissive for non-convertible debt securities of a bank to which the Bank Act, Canada applies. No accredited/eligible investor or purchaser wealth test is imposed.

A. Bank of China [Canada] is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors in Ontario is the textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank debt exemption. The large retail pool is immaterial. A is unambiguously compliant.

B. The stated issuer is JPMorgan Chase, the U.S. parent, with a general Canadian retail bond offering. On the conventional NI 45-106 s.1.1 reading the exemption is limited to debt of a bank to which the Bank Act applies, i.e. a Schedule I/II/III Bank Act bank or an authorized foreign bank acting through its Canadian presence. No Bank Act issuer or Canadian branch issuance is made out on the facts and no other exemption is made out. B is a prospectus distribution on the majority statutory reading. The “any bank” textual reading advanced by Colleague 6 is the outlier.

* Private issuer
NI 45-106 s.2.4 is issuer based. The issuer must be a private issuer, non-reporting <50 holders worldwide, ≤50 purchasers in 12 months and no advertising. There is no accredited/eligible investor financial test in s.2.4.

C. The fact pattern states the distribution is by a private issuer to a single non-connected purchaser. Salary $35k and net assets $10k defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM eligible investor and are the intended distractor for s.2.4. On the stated private-issuer predicate the trade is capable of/ is made under s.2.4, subject to the usual private issuer / no advertising / purchaser count conditions which are not negatived on the facts. C is compliant under s.2.4 with the financials being irrelevant to s.2.4.

* Bank equity v bank debt
The financial institution exemption in s.2.35/2.36 is debt only.

D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I Bank Act bank. Its non-convertible debt would be within s.2.35/2.36; its equity is not. A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is non-exempt. The issuer-based rationale does not convert s.2.35/2.36 into an equity exemption.

* Cooperative credit association / caisse populaire
NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based, issuer based exemption for distributions of securities by a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire to its members. Purchaser wealth is irrelevant.

E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. The exemption is real and purchaser wealth would be irrelevant, but it is membership based. The facts as worded state “a large number of retail investors” and do not expressly state a members-only distribution to members of the association. On a strict reading of the facts as given the members-only condition is not proved. On the conventional teaching membership assumption E would be compliant, the $0 net assets/unemployed fact being irrelevant.

On the facts as stated without additional factual assumptions the only unassailable, archetypal compliant transaction in the set is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. On a straight NI 45-106 reading C is also compliant under s.2.4 private issuer, the financials being a distractor, and E is compliant only on the standard membership assumption. B and D are non-exempt on the majority statutory reading.

3.text:
Ontario s.53 OSA is displaced as of Jan 2020 by NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501 and Ont Reg 1015.

Bank non-convertible debt

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is an issuer based, retail permissive, purchaser condition free exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, Canada applies.  “Bank” in NI 45-106 s.1.1 is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada. The exemption is debt only and there is no accredited/eligible investor or purchaser wealth test.

* A. Bank of China [Canada] is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors in Ontario is the textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank debt exemption. The large retail pool is immaterial. A is unassailable.

* B. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent holding company. On the facts as stated there is no Bank Act issuer, no Canadian authorized foreign bank Canadian presence issuer and no guarantee by a Canadian bank made out, and no other exemption is made out. The s.2.35/2.36 exemption is limited to debt of a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The issuer-based retail permissive rationale for A does not convert the statutory Bank Act filter into “any bank”. B is a prospectus distribution in Ontario on the conventional statutory reading.

Private issuer

NI 45-106 s.2.4 is an issuer based private issuer exemption. The issuer must be a private issuer, i.e. non-reporting and <50 holders worldwide, the distribution must be to ≤50 purchasers in 12 months and not by advertising. There is no accredited/eligible investor or minimum amount financial test in s.2.4.

The $35k salary / $10k net assets figures defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 Ontario OM/eligible investor and are the intended distractor for s.2.4.

* C. The fact pattern states the distribution is by a private issuer to a single non-connected purchaser. On that stated predicate the trade is capable of/ is made under s.2.4. It would not be exempt under s.2.3 or s.2.9, which is why the financials are present. C is compliant under s.2.4 subject to the usual private issuer / no advertising / purchaser count conditions which are not negatived on the facts.

Bank equity v bank debt

The financial institution exemption in s.2.35/2.36 is debt only. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not caught.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I bank. Its non-convertible debt would be within s.2.35/2.36; its equity is not. A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is a prospectus distribution. The issuer-based rationale does not convert s.2.35/2.36 into a securities of a bank exemption.

Co-operative credit association / caisse populaire

NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based, issuer based exemption for distributions of securities by a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire to its members. Purchaser wealth is irrelevant.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. On the conventional teaching the member share offering is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ net worth/employment so the $0 net assets/unemployed fact is irrelevant. The residual factual point is the members-only condition. The fact pattern is worded as “a large number of retail investors” rather than “members”. On the standard membership assumption E is compliant under s.2.34; on a strict reading of the facts as written the membership condition is not proved.

On that statutory reading the only distribution made out without any factual assumption is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. C is compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with the financials as a distractor, and E is compliant under s.2.34 on the usual member-based reading, while B and D are non-compliant on the majority Bank Act and debt-only readings.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Thanks everyone for the very careful statutory mapping – the issuer-based / retail-permissive framing for NI 45-106 s.2.35, OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.36 and OSA s.73 is what I am taking away from R3 and it is why the purchaser wealth / zero net assets / unemployed facts are being treated as distractors for the bank examples.

With that framing in place I am still uneasy about how decisive the debt-only gloss is being treated for D, and how much that gloss is then being used to make A look unassailable.

We all agree Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I Bank Act bank and that Bank of China [Canada] is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. We also agree the exemption is issuer based and contains no accredited / eligible investor or purchaser financial test. The big retail pool and the $0 net assets / unemployed purchaser are immaterial on that issuer-based logic.

That is why the equity v debt line matters so much. Colleague 4’s question on the precise wording is, in my view, the hinge. The teaching version is often paraphrased as “non-convertible debt securities of a bank / loan corporation / trust company / insurance company”. If the text in NI 45-106 s.2.35(1) / Rule 45-501 s.2.36(1) as in force in January 2020 is expressly limited to non-convertible debt securities, then Fairstone shares are out. If the operative Ontario formulation is being read as “securities of a bank” with the debt limitation being a policy gloss imported from the commercial paper context, then Fairstone’s share distribution sits on the same issuer-based, purchaser-condition-free footing as Bank of China Canada’s bond distribution. The purchaser’s $0 net assets and unemployment would be irrelevant for Fairstone on exactly the same logic that makes the retail bond offering for Bank of China Canada look clean.

I would like us to lock down the exact January 2020 wording of s.2.35(1)/s.2.36(1) before we treat the debt-only reading as dispositive for D. On an issuer-based reading, D is at least textually comparable to A, and the only material difference we are imposing is equity vs debt.

That also helps put the other options in perspective. E is the classic cooperative credit association / caisse populaire member share exemption under NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 and purchaser wealth is indeed irrelevant there, but the fact pattern as written says “a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed” and does not state a members-only distribution to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée. Without the membership condition made out on the facts as stated, E is weaker than the pure issuer-based bank analysis.

C is a useful illustration of the s.2.4 private issuer distractor – the $35k salary / $10k net assets are clearly there to defeat s.2.3 and s.2.9 – but the facts do not establish the NI 45-106 private issuer predicates, e.g. non-reporting issuer, <50 holders worldwide, no advertising, ≤50 purchasers in 12 months. The financials are a distractor, they are not proof the s.2.4 conditions are met.

B remains the Canadian Bank Act issuer point. With the issuer-based logic we are using for A, the question is whether we are reading a Canadian incorporation / Schedule I/II/III limitation into s.2.35/2.36 or sticking with the statutory elements of debt of a bank issued without a prospectus to retail.

Given that, I think we should not dismiss D as obviously non-exempt while treating A as obviously exempt on the basis of a debt-only policy gloss that we have not verified against the January 2020 text. Thanks for the detailed close reads – the issuer-based, retail-permissive, no purchaser wealth test framing for the financial institution carve-out is now the shared anchor in the room and that’s the right anchor.

I agree with Colleagues 1,2,3 and 5 that NI 45-106 s.2.35 / OSC Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer based and not conditioned on accredited / eligible investor status or on net worth. That is why the large retail pool and the zero net assets / unemployed purchaser facts are properly treated as distractors for a bank debt analysis.

JPMorgan Chase is a bank and the securities at issue are bonds, i.e. non-convertible debt securities, distributed without a prospectus to a large number of Canadian investors. The elements of the exemption — bank issuer, debt security, non-prospectus retail distribution — are all made out on the facts.

The Schedule I/II/III gloss is the usual teaching shorthand for the definition of “bank” in NI 45-106 s.1.1, but the exemption text itself does not on its face condition the exemption on Canadian incorporation or on a Canadian authorized branch issuance. In an issuer-based, purchaser-condition-free regime, the textual distinction between Bank of China Canada and JPMorgan Chase is incorporation, not the statutory elements of debt of a bank issued without a prospectus to retail. On a straight statutory reading B is textually as clean an illustration of the retail-permissive bank debt exemption as A, and it tests the foreign bank extension of the same issuer-based logic we are all using for A.

The fact pattern states “a large number of retail investors, one of whom has zero dollars of net assets and is unemployed” and does not state a members-only distribution to members of Caisse populaire acadienne ltée. C is a good private issuer s.2.4 distractor — the $35k salary / $10k net assets clearly defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 OM eligible investor — but the facts do not establish the NI 45-106 private issuer predicates: non-reporting, <50 holders worldwide, no advertising and ≤50 purchasers in 12 months. D remains equity, not debt, and the majority position that s.2.35/2.36 is debt only is well supported; Fairstone Bank common shares to retail including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no other exemption is made out.

Ontario s.53 OSA is displaced as of Jan 2020 by NI 45-106, OSC Rule 45-501 and Ont Reg 1015.

Bank non-convertible debt

NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is an issuer based, retail permissive, purchaser condition free exemption for non-convertible debt securities of a bank, loan corporation, trust company or insurance company to which the Bank Act, Canada applies.  “Bank” in NI 45-106 s.1.1 is a bank listed in Schedule I, II or III of the Bank Act, Canada. The exemption is debt only and there is no accredited/eligible investor or purchaser wealth test.

* A. Bank of China [Canada] is a Schedule II Bank Act bank. A non-prospectus distribution of its bonds to retail investors in Ontario is the textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank debt exemption. The large retail pool is immaterial. A is unassailable.

* B. JPMorgan Chase is the U.S. parent holding company. On the facts as stated there is no Bank Act issuer, no Canadian authorized foreign bank Canadian presence issuer and no guarantee by a Canadian bank made out, and no other exemption is made out. The s.2.35/2.36 exemption is limited to debt of a bank to which the Bank Act applies. The issuer-based retail permissive rationale for A does not convert the statutory Bank Act filter into “any bank”. B is a prospectus distribution in Ontario on the conventional statutory reading.

Private issuer

NI 45-106 s.2.4 is an issuer based private issuer exemption. The issuer must be a private issuer, i.e. non-reporting and <50 holders worldwide, the distribution must be to ≤50 purchasers in 12 months and not by advertising. There is no accredited/eligible investor or minimum amount financial test in s.2.4.

The $35k salary / $10k net assets figures defeat s.2.3 accredited investor and s.2.9 Ontario OM/eligible investor and are the intended distractor for s.2.4.

* C. The fact pattern states the distribution is by a private issuer to a single non-connected purchaser. On that stated predicate the trade is capable of/ is made under s.2.4. It would not be exempt under s.2.3 or s.2.9, which is why the financials are present. C is compliant under s.2.4 subject to the usual private issuer / no advertising / purchaser count conditions which are not negatived on the facts.

Bank equity v bank debt

The financial institution exemption in s.2.35/2.36 is debt only. Equity of a Bank Act bank is not caught.

* D. Fairstone Bank of Canada is a Schedule I bank. Its non-convertible debt would be within s.2.35/2.36; its equity is not. A non-prospectus distribution of common shares to a broad retail pool including a $0 net assets unemployed purchaser is not bank debt and no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption is made out on the facts. D is a prospectus distribution. The issuer-based rationale does not convert s.2.35/2.36 into a securities of a bank exemption.

Co-operative credit association / caisse populaire

NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 is a member based, issuer based exemption for distributions of securities by a cooperative credit association/caisse populaire to its members. Purchaser wealth is irrelevant.

* E. Caisse populaire acadienne ltée is a federally incorporated caisse populaire. On the conventional teaching the member share offering is prospectus exempt irrespective of members’ net worth/employment so the $0 net assets/unemployed fact is irrelevant. The residual factual point is the members-only condition. The fact pattern is worded as “a large number of retail investors” rather than “members”. On the standard membership assumption E is compliant under s.2.34; on a strict reading of the facts as written the membership condition is not proved.

On that statutory reading the only distribution made out without any factual assumption is A, the Canadian bank non-convertible debt distribution to retail. C is compliant under s.2.4 private issuer with the financials as a distractor, and E is compliant under s.2.34 on the usual member-based reading, while B and D are non-compliant on the majority Bank Act and debt-only readings.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: Shared baseline unchanged: Ontario prospectus s.53 OSA displaced Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015. Financial institution exemptions are issuer based, retail permissive, no purchaser wealth test.

Bank debt
* A – Bank of China (Canada) bonds to retail without prospectus. Uncontested compliant. Bank of China Canada is Schedule II Bank Act bank; NI 45-106 s.2.35 and Rule 45-501 s.2.36 non-convertible debt of a Bank Act bank is issuer based, retail permitted, no accredited/eligible test. Large retail pool immaterial.
* B – JPMorgan Chase bonds to large Canadian investors without prospectus. Majority 1,2,3,5: exemption limited to debt securities of a bank to which the Bank Act applies, i.e. Schedule I/II/III Canadian bank or authorised foreign bank acting through Canadian presence. JPMorgan Chase is U.S. parent, no Canadian Bank Act issuer or branch issuance made out, no other exemption stated → non-exempt. Minority Colleague 6 persists: s.2.35/2.36 is textually “debt securities of a bank”, issuer based and purchaser-condition free, does not on its face require Canadian incorporation; on straight reading B is as compliant as A. Disagreement remains on foreign-bank scope.

Private issuer / accredited / OM
* C – shares by private issuer to non-connected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k. Majority 1,2,3,5 in current round now treat financials as distractor and rely on NI 45-106 s.2.4 private issuer exemption: issuer based, no accredited/eligible financial test, 50 purchaser/no-advertising conditions not negatived. On that reading C is capable of being exempt; would not be exempt under s.2.3 accredited investor or s.2.9 eligible investor/OM. Colleague 4 continues factual predicate challenge: facts do not establish private issuer status in NI 45-106 sense <50 holders non-reporting nor advertising limits, so exemption not made out on facts. Change from round 0 accredited-only view now largely abandoned by majority.

Bank equity
* D – Fairstone Bank of Canada shares without prospectus to broad retail including $0 net assets unemployed purchaser. Majority 1,2,3,5: financial institution exemption is debt only; equity not caught by s.2.35/2.36; no accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount exemption made out → non-exempt. Colleague 4 dissent persists: issuer-based rationale of bank exemption suggests securities of a bank not debt-limited; purchaser wealth irrelevant; on that reading D would be compliant irrespective of equity status. Outlier issuer-based securities view remains.

Credit union / co-operative
* E – shares by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée to large retail pool including $0 net assets unemployed purchaser. Majority 1,2,3,5: prospectus exemption NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34 / OSA s.73 for distributions by Canadian co-operative credit association/caisse populaire to members, issuer and member based, no accredited/eligible test, purchaser wealth irrelevant. Residual caveat: exemption is member based. Fact pattern states “retail investors” not expressly members. Colleague 4 and 5 flag membership condition; if membership not established exemption may fail. On conventional teaching membership assumed.

Unresolved / to track
* Scope of bank debt exemption for authorized foreign banks vs U.S. parent issuer for B, and whether statutory text requires Canadian Bank Act bank.
* Whether private issuer exemption s.2.4 can be relied on for C given lack of explicit facts on <50 holders, reporting status, no-advertising/50 purchaser limits.
* Whether credit union exemption for E requires membership and whether fact pattern satisfies it; factual wording “retail investors” vs “members”.
* Debt vs equity scope of bank exemption driving D disagreement, and Colleague 4’s issuer-based securities reading.

Current working synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant. E is widely treated as compliant under co-operative member exemption subject to membership condition. C is majority-leaning compliant under private issuer exemption with financials as distractor, though factual predicates contested. B and D are majority non-compliant; B has persistent minority compliant view on foreign bank scope, D has minority issuer-based securities compliant view.

reflection_text.1:
Ontario prospectus s.53 OSA displaced Jan 2020 by NI 45-106 / OSC Rule 45-501 / Ont Reg 1015.

Bank non-convertible debt exemption NI 45-106 s.2.35 / Rule 45-501 s.2.36 / OSA s.73 is issuer-based, retail-permissive, purchaser-condition-free for non-convertible debt of a bank/loan/trust/insurance to which the Bank Act Canada applies. NI 45-106 definition of “bank” = Schedule I/II/III Bank Act bank. Exemption is debt only on majority reading.

A. Bank of China (Canada) Schedule II Bank Act bank, bonds to retail. Unanimous majority: textbook s.2.35/2.36 bank-debt exemption, unambiguously compliant. No serious dispute.

B. JPMorgan Chase bonds to large Canadian retail pool. Majority 1,2,3,5: exemption requires Bank Act bank / authorized foreign bank Canadian presence; U.S. parent on facts as stated is outside s.2.35/2.36 and no other exemption made out → prospectus required, non-compliant. Minority Colleague 6: reads s.2.35/2.36 as issuer-based “debt securities of a bank” with no Canada-only incorporation condition; JPMorgan Chase is a bank and bonds are debt → would be exempt. Disagreement persists on foreign bank scope / Canadian nexus.

C. Private issuer shares to non-connected individual, salary $35k, net assets $10k CAD. Accredited investor NI 31-103 and eligible investor NI 45-106 s.2.9 not met. Majority 1,2,3 in current round: NI 45-106 s.2.4 private issuer exemption is issuer-based, no accredited/eligible financial test, ≤50 purchasers / no advertising conditions. Facts state “private issuer” and one purchaser; salary/net assets are distractors for accredited/OM analysis. Hence capable/compliant under s.2.4. Remaining concern raised by Colleagues 4,5: private issuer predicates – non-reporting, <50 holders worldwide, no advertising, ≤50 purchasers – not expressly proven on facts; financials are distractor but not proof conditions met.

D. Shares without prospectus by Fairstone Bank of Canada to large retail pool including purchaser $0 net assets unemployed. Majority 1,2,3,5: s.2.35/2.36 is debt only. Equity not covered. No accredited/eligible/OM/minimum amount/family friends exemption made out → prospectus required, non-compliant. Colleague 4 dissent: issuer-based rationale for bank exemption should attach to Fairstone as Schedule I bank irrespective of debt vs equity; purchaser wealth irrelevant. Core disagreement is debt-only vs “securities of a bank” reading of s.2.35/2.36. Colleague 4 requests exact wording of s.2.35(1)/s.2.36(1) to confirm debt limitation.

E. Shares without prospectus by Caisse populaire acadienne ltée to large retail pool including purchaser $0 net assets unemployed. Majority 2,3: cooperative credit association / caisse populaire member-share exemption NI 45-106 s.2.34 / Rule 45-501 s.2.34, OSA s.73, issuer and member based, no accredited/eligible test; purchaser wealth irrelevant. Colleague 4/5 note membership requirement not stated; facts say “large number of retail investors” not “members”. Without express members-only condition made out on facts as stated, s.2.34 not proved; conventional membership assumption makes E compliant.

Unresolved / tracking:
- Foreign bank scope for bank-debt exemption: Canadian Bank Act bank required or any bank sufficient? Majority = Canadian nexus; minority Colleague 6 = any bank.
- Bank exemption covers equity? Majority = debt only; minority Colleague 4 = securities of bank, issuer-based.
- Membership condition for E: is it satisfied on facts? Majority assumes yes; Colleagues 4,5 flag missing.
- Private issuer exemption for C: are issuer status/conditions established, or are financials merely distractors vs evidence issuer is not private? Majority treats as compliant under s.2.4.

Current best synthesis: A is unambiguously compliant archetypal example. B is majority non-compliant, minority compliant. D is majority non-compliant, minority compliant. E is majority compliant under cooperative member exemption subject to membership assumption. C is majority now viewed as compliant under s.2.4 private issuer, financial details distractors.
